name: vscode-serial-port
description: Full-featured serial port tool for VS Code: monitor, send/receive (hex or ASCII), RTS/DTR control, multiple ports in parallel, log-to-file, and reusable send templates. Works transparently from WSL windows against physical Windows ports.

untrustedWorkspaces.description: This extension only talks to physical serial ports and writes log files; it does not execute any workspace code.

virtualWorkspaces.description: Serial port I/O and log files always resolve against the local/UI-side filesystem regardless of workspace type; recording to a virtual workspace folder is not supported.

serialPort.defaultBaudRate.description: Default baud rate used when a newly added port is opened.

serialPort.defaultDataBits.description: Default data bits used when a newly added port is opened.

serialPort.defaultParity.description: Default parity used when a newly added port is opened.

serialPort.defaultStopBits.description: Default stop bits used when a newly added port is opened.

serialPort.defaultHexSend.description: Default Hex Send state used when a newly added port is opened.

serialPort.defaultHexRecv.description: Default Hex Receive state used when a newly added port is opened.

serialPort.defaultShowTimestamp.description: Default Show Timestamp state used when a newly added port is opened.

enumDescriptions: Send exactly what was typed, with no terminator appended.
Append a carriage return and line feed (\r\n).
serialPort.defaultLineEnding.description: Line terminator appended to every ASCII send (typed lines and ASCII templates; never hex sends), used when a newly added port is opened. Most embedded consoles — ESP-IDF, Zephyr shell, AT-command modems — do nothing until a command line is terminated. Each session can override this from its card.

serialPort.defaultDeviceConsole.markdownDescription: Default **Device Console** state used when a newly added port is opened. Device Console hands the terminal over to the device: every keystroke (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+D, Tab, arrow keys) is sent the instant you press it, and the device controls the screen itself — what a MicroPython REPL, a Zephyr or ESP-IDF shell, a bootloader menu or any full-screen device UI needs. Off, the terminal edits a line locally (history, cursor keys, Ctrl+L) and sends it on Enter. Recording is unaffected either way.

serialPort.compactTimestamps.description: Render timestamps in the terminal and log file as the time of day only ("20:58:48.375") instead of the default month-day-and-time ("09-05 20:58:48.375"). Neither form carries a year or a UTC offset — those are constant for a session and appear on the file's "# ---" banner. Only affects lines rendered/logged after the setting changes; already-rendered lines are never altered.

serialPort.detectSeverity.description: Recognise the log-level prefix at the start of each received line — ESP-IDF ("E (1234) tag:"), Zephyr ("<err>"), Linux printk ("<3>"), Android ("E/Tag(123):"), generic "[ERROR]"/"ERROR:", and ESP32 crash markers — falling back to the line's own ANSI colour. The terminal colours the row to match and the annotated log fills in the level column of its header. Received lines only: what you send is a command, not a log record.

enumDescriptions: One readable line per device line, each with a [timestamp MODE DIRECTION] header and, when severity detection is on, a normalised level token. Written to *.serial.log.
Byte-exact capture of the wire in arrival order — nothing added, stripped or transformed. Written to *.raw.log.
serialPort.logFormat.description: How a recorded log file is written. Read when recording starts, so changing this never leaves one file holding a mix of both formats; the new value applies the next time recording begins.

serialPort.messageGapMs.description: Milliseconds of quiet time on the wire after which an unterminated line is surfaced anyway — a device that prints a prompt like "esp32> " and waits sends no newline, so without this the partial line would be held indefinitely. Also the coalescing window for hex-mode receive, where the byte stream has no line structure to split on.

serialPort.saveLogAt.description: Folder to write serial session log files to. The literal ${workspaceFolder} token is resolved to the first workspace folder at log-write time (falling back to the extension's global storage folder when no workspace is open); any other value is used as-is as an absolute path.

serialPort.txColor.description: Terminal color for transmitted (TX) bytes, as a CSS hex color.

serialPort.rxColor.description: Terminal color for received (RX) bytes, as a CSS hex color.

ERROR.description: Colour for lines detected as ERROR.

WARN.description: Colour for lines detected as WARN.

INFO.description: Colour for lines detected as INFO.

DEBUG.description: Colour for lines detected as DEBUG.

TRACE.description: Colour for lines detected as TRACE (ESP-IDF verbose, Zephyr <dbg>).

serialPort.severityColors.markdownDescription: Colour of each detected log level, as a CSS hex colour (`#rrggbb`). One palette drives both surfaces: in the terminal it colours the whole row, and in an open `*.serial.log` it colours the level token in the header (with ERROR and WARN also marked in the scrollbar's overview ruler). Set a level to an empty string to turn its override off — that row then keeps the ordinary TX/RX colour, which is what you want if you find recolouring every INFO line too noisy. Editable from the panel's **Default Settings › Level Colours** section. Requires `#serialPort.detectSeverity#`.

serialPort.sendTemplates.description: Reusable send templates shown in the Send Templates panel section.

editor.tokenColorCustomizations.comment: Fallback colours for a recorded log's header, for the window before this extension activates. No built-in theme styles the 'log.*' scopes, so without these the level would be theme-foreground on every line, and TX/RX would take whatever a theme happens to give 'keyword'/'support.class' — usually something loud and unrelated. Once the extension is active it decorates the level token, the direction token and the payload from serialPort.severityColors + serialPort.txColor/rxColor instead, and a decoration paints over a token colour — so those settings are what you actually see, and these values only need to match their defaults. The mode column ('ASC'/'HEX') is deliberately dimmed rather than coloured: it repeats on every line and carries the least information in the header. These are contributed as defaults: a user's own editor.tokenColorCustomizations replaces them entirely.

scripts.pretest: npm run compile-tests && npm run compile && npm run lint
